# The walkdown record format

<!-- Generated by `pnpm guide` from src/reference/. Do not edit by hand. -->

A walkdown is one record of one merged change: a tree of claims, each with a title, a
body of markdown and figures, the hunks it accounts for, and the claims under it.
`walkdown check <folder>` validates one; `walkdown reference` prints the same field
tables as below.

A record is a folder, named for the central claim’s id. Its `index.md` is the central
claim. A claim with no supporting claims is one file, `<id>.md`; a claim with them is a
folder, `<id>/`, holding its own `index.md` and a file or folder for each, listed in order
by its header’s `claims`. A file or folder name is the claim’s whole id.

Each file is a YAML header between `---` lines, then a markdown body. In the body, a
fence opened at the start of its line with `yaml` and a figure type, ```` ```yaml flow ````,
is a figure, and its YAML holds the figure’s fields; everything else is markdown. A
figure whose text holds a line of three backticks opens with four.

Where a paragraph lists things, write them as a bulleted list, one to a line, in any
markdown: a body, a `line`, a caption, a table cell.

Aim for about three figures that explain the change, not counting the header. The one
that tells the change best goes in full in the central claim’s body, on the top page;
any other has to earn its place. Examples and evidence do not count against them: show
a claim with an excerpt, a case, a measurement or a snippet wherever you can, and
annotate it wherever a line has a decent reason to be pointed at.

Every row says, in its title and `line`, why it is worth opening and how it bears on
the change, not only what the code does. Write it in plain technical English for a
reader who knows the codebase at a high level, and may know parts of it deeply, but has
only a passing familiarity with this area. Wherever the area is not obvious, give
`context`: where the code runs in the pipeline (“during document sync, when checking
whether content changed”), not its direct caller. Never trade clarity for brevity: a
few more words that make a row understandable beat a terse phrase the reader can only
decode by already knowing the mechanism.

`line` may be left out where the title says all there is: an item in a list of cases,
a file that is only renamed. A claim with a title alone, and no body, code or supporting
claims, draws as one row that opens nothing and keeps its kind. A row that opens a
page keeps its line, since that is where it says why it is worth opening.

A page with many rows can group them: a `- section: <heading>` item in `claims`
heads the rows listed after it, up to the next section. The top page’s sections also
label the outline a reader moves around the record by.

A word the reader would otherwise have to look up goes in `glossary.yaml`, beside the
root `index.md`: its term, the aliases the prose also writes it as, and a definition.
The page dots every occurrence in its prose and shows the definition on hover, and a
glossary page lists each term with the claims that use it. Define the words this area
uses that a reader new to it would not know, not the codebase’s everyday words.

## Example

```
orkestra-ts-78/gate/gate.checks.md
orkestra-ts-78/gate/index.md
orkestra-ts-78/gate/tables/gate.yaml
orkestra-ts-78/glossary.yaml
orkestra-ts-78/index.md
orkestra-ts-78/route/index.md
orkestra-ts-78/route/payloads/asks.yaml
orkestra-ts-78/route/route.artifact.md
orkestra-ts-78/route/route.parse.md
orkestra-ts-78/route/route.questions.md
orkestra-ts-78/step/index.md
orkestra-ts-78/step/shots/narrow.svg
orkestra-ts-78/step/shots/wide.svg
orkestra-ts-78/step/step.lead/card.svg
orkestra-ts-78/step/step.lead/d.order.md
orkestra-ts-78/step/step.lead/index.md
orkestra-ts-78/step/step.plan.md
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/index.md`

````markdown
---
# The root index.md is the central claim, drawn as the top page. The folder's name,
# orkestra-ts-78, is its id. Cut down from fixtures/orkestra-ts-78 and fixtures/orkestra-ts-91;
# `pnpm test` checks it.
walkdown: 1 # the format version
slug: orkestra-ts-78 # the page's name: publish puts it at <repository>/<slug>.html
# The diff the record walks, base..head, as full SHAs. Leave base out for a snapshot.
base: 17fa58df4bba015d4eb5a03a710c8cb39464051a
head: 291b2ffe9919e661da2b06ae1240ef0555499e7d
# The header, drawn at the head of the top page, the same on every record
prs: # optional: the pull requests, each drawn as its number
  - https://github.com/tiniest-fox/orkestra-ts/pull/78
change: fix # optional: fix, feature or refactor
motivation: >- # why it was made, in a sentence or two
  A trak that opened on a question had its steps answer the question instead of doing
  their own job.
before: >- # a sentence each; the body's figure shows it in full
  A step's prompt opened on the trak's opening message.
after: A step's prompt opens on its own instruction.
title: Open each step's prompt on its own instruction, not the trak's opening message
line: >- # one sentence under the title
  The reordering puts the step's job first, and the renamed heading makes the message
  read as where the work started.
questions: # for the crit; the page never shows them
  - What does a step's prompt open on now, and where did its instruction sit before?
claims: # supporting claims, drawn as rows: step/, route/ and gate/ beside this file
  - step
  - section: After the turn # optional: a heading over the rows listed after it
  - route
  - gate
---

```yaml shift
# a figure: yaml, then its type. `>-` keeps a leading backtick and ` #` from breaking the YAML
before: >-
  A step's prompt opened on `# The request` and the trak's opening message.
after: >-
  A step's prompt opens on `# This step` and its instruction.
```
````

### `orkestra-ts-78/step/index.md`

````markdown
---
# A claim with supporting claims is a folder, and its index.md lists them.
context: [starting a step, composing its prompt] # optional: where in the pipeline it runs
title: The step prompt opens on its own instruction
line: The instruction moves from about 1,900 words down to line 1.
claims: [step.plan, step.lead] # step.plan.md and step.lead/, beside this file
---

```yaml flow
# The fence's second word names the figure; its body is the figure's fields, as YAML.
steps: [step.plan, step.lead] # this claim's own claims. No hops: joined in the order listed
code: # the code a step runs, by the step's name: drawn in full under its row
  step.lead:
    lines: [src/prompts/templates/step.md#1]
    key: [src/prompts/templates/step.md#1:4] # the lines a map's station shows: one to three
```

A plain `yaml` fence, or one in any other language, is prose:

```yaml
not: a figure
```

```yaml table
columns: [surface, what this change puts there]
rows:
  - [Prompt, '`# This step` and the instruction are the first lines']
  - [UI, Nothing.]
caption: Every surface the change could reach.
```
````

### `orkestra-ts-78/step/step.plan.md`

`````markdown
---
# A claim with no supporting claims is one file, named for its id.
title: The instruction is written into the plan
# `(#step.lead)` names a claim anywhere in the record: a click opens it.
line: The composer writes one instruction per step, which [the prompt now leads with](#step.lead); nothing here changed.
---

````yaml excerpt
# Four backticks, because the text holds a line of three that would end a shorter fence.
src: captured # or `derived`: worked out from the code
where: quiet-emerald-capybara · log.jsonl line 27
text: |-
  { "agent": "ui-prototype", "instruction": "Prototype the pitch card…" }
  ```
````

```yaml gallery
groups: # named groups, each drawn under its heading, three shots across
  - name: The card
    caption: The instruction leads at either width.
    shots:
      - label: desk · 1440 # what tells this shot from the others
        src: shots/wide.svg # relative to this file
        alt: The pitch card at desk width, with the step's instruction on its first line.
      - label: phone · 390
        src: shots/narrow.svg

        caption: Drawn only when the shot is opened full screen.
```
`````

### `orkestra-ts-78/step/step.lead/index.md`

````markdown
---
title: '`# This step` and the instruction are lines 1 and 3'
line: '`# The request` and the opening message used to lead.'
code: # hunk ids from `walkdown hunks`
  - src/prompts/templates/step.md#1 # a whole hunk: path#n
  - src/prompts/templates/step.md#2:1-27 # lines 1–27 of that hunk
claims: [d.order]
---

```yaml before-after
how: Rendered through buildStepPrompt at the parent commit and at this one.
before:
  where: step.md at 17fa58df
  text: |-
    # The request

    Remind me: did we add the ability for the composer to pitch a new trak?
    […]
after:
  where: step.md at 291b2ffe
  text: |-
    # This step

    Prototype the pitch card…
```

```yaml snippet
# Code from git, never pasted: `:1-3,6` keeps lines 1–3 and 6, and draws ⋯ for 4–5.
code: # a list item, not `[...]`, whose commas would split the id
  - src/prompts/templates/step.md#2:1-3,6
annotations: # this claim's own claims, each drawn beside the lines it explains
  - { lines: 1-2, claim: d.order } # lines as `walkdown hunks` numbers them
```

```yaml image
src: card.svg # relative to this file
alt: The pitch card, with the step's instruction on its first line.
```
````

### `orkestra-ts-78/step/step.lead/d.order.md`

```markdown
---
kind: tradeoff # tradeoff, open, risk, breaking or measured; none is plain
title: Reorder the prompt and rename one heading, and add nothing
line: The smallest change that puts the step's job first.
# One markdown block and nothing else below: its row shows it in place, not on a page.
---

**Set aside:** passing the plan title into both prompts as their heading.
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/route/index.md`

````markdown
---
title: 'The envelope routes the step: to the gate or to a person'
line: Two ways out of a turn, and each is a case a reader can pick.
claims: [route.parse, route.artifact, route.questions]
---

```yaml flow
# A fork: drawn as a map. A hop back to an earlier step would be a loop. A flow that forks
# has lenses, one way through to each, and its steps say nothing of the hops: the labels are
# written on the map.
steps: [route.parse, route.artifact, route.questions]
hops:
  - { from: route.parse, to: route.artifact, label: artifact }
  - { from: route.parse, to: route.questions, label: questions }
# Lenses: the cases a reader can pick, each lighting its steps. The first is picked on open.
# A lens may carry a payload, as a flow with none may. A flow carries payloads or step code,
# never both: `step/` carries code.
lenses:
  - name: asks first
    steps: [route.parse, route.questions]
    payload: payloads/asks.yaml # a YAML file beside this one: the data the lens carries
    # A lens whose payload comes round a loop may say, by step, what a step reached again
    # does differently: `again: { route.parse: reads the answers this time }`.
  # A lens lights the hops its payload takes; one with no payload lights every hop between
  # its steps, unless it lists them as `hops: [{ from: route.parse, to: route.artifact }]`.
  - name: files at once
    steps: [route.parse, route.artifact]
```
````

### `orkestra-ts-78/route/route.parse.md`

```markdown
---
title: The envelope is checked against the step's contract
line: Every required section present, every question with options.
---
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/route/route.artifact.md`

```markdown
---
title: An artifact is filed as the step's document
line: Sections by title, with requirements beside them.
---
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/route/route.questions.md`

```markdown
---
title: Questions stop the step in front of a person
line: Each question with its options drawn as choices.
---
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/gate/index.md`

````markdown
---
title: The gate lets a finished step go on only when every check passes
line: One question, asked once the checks have run, and two ways out of it.
claims: [gate.checks]
---

```yaml walkthrough
# A decision the reader walks one step at a time: which way it goes, and why. For a thing
# moving through the system, in what order, draw a flow. A step with no option out is an
# outcome; a step with several needs a `label` on each.
steps:
  - gate.checks
  - { label: every check passed? }
  - { label: advance }
  - { label: send back }
hops:
  - from: gate.checks
    to: every check passed?
    means: The exit codes are in; the gate reads them.
  - from: every check passed?
    to: advance
    label: passed
    rule: exit 0 for every check # drawn on the card, and after the pick
    means: The step's work goes on to the next step.
    # What the pick pins down in the table, by `row.column`, a column, a row or a field
    narrows: { exit: '0', route: advance }
  - from: every check passed?
    to: send back
    label: failed
    rule: any check exits non-zero
    means: The step is sent back with the failing check's output.
    narrows: { verify.exit: '≠ 0', route: send back }
# code: { gate.checks: { key: [src/gate.ts#1:4] } } — a step's key lines, and only those
table: tables/gate.yaml # a YAML file beside this one: the table the decision reads
```
````

### `orkestra-ts-78/gate/gate.checks.md`

```markdown
---
title: Every check the step is held to runs before the gate decides
line: The checks run in the order the step names them, and each one's exit code is kept.
---

- A check that fails does not stop the ones after it.
- Output is kept only for a check that fails.
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/route/payloads/asks.yaml`

```yaml
# A payload file: not a claim, so no header. Its stages are the payload after each step,
# in the order it passes them; each is diffed against the stage whose step handed it on.
input:
  value: '`envelope: null`' # one mono line, drawn as IN beside START
  data: { envelope: null, asked: 0 }
stages:
  - step: route.parse
    does: reads the turn's last block as its envelope
    value: '`envelope: questions`'
    data: { envelope: questions, asked: 0 }
  - step: route.questions
    does: draws each question as choices and stops the step
    value: '`asked: 2`'
    data: { envelope: questions, asked: 2 }
outcome: the step waits for a person to answer
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/gate/tables/gate.yaml`

```yaml
# The table a walkthrough decides on: rows and typed columns, what each step reads and
# writes, and one real example per outcome.
input:
  - { name: step, holds: string } # a line over the table
heading: check
columns:
  - { name: exit, holds: exit code } # drawn in italics until a pick pins it
  - { name: took, holds: seconds, range: 0 – 600 } # or its range, when it has one
rows:
  - { name: verify }
  - { name: lint, cells: [exit] } # the columns this row has; the rest draw —
fields:
  - { name: route, holds: route } # a line under the table
steps: # what each step reads and writes, tinted while it is on screen
  gate.checks: { reads: [step], writes: [exit, took] }
  every check passed?: { reads: [exit], writes: [route] }
examples: # one real case per outcome, drawn when the walk reaches it
  advance:
    input: 3-build
    values: 'verify 0, lint 0'
    outcome: The trak moves on to its review.
  send back:
    input: 3-build
    values: 'verify 1, lint 0'
    outcome: The build step runs again with the failing output in its prompt.
```

### `orkestra-ts-78/glossary.yaml`

```yaml
# Optional: the words this record defines, as a list beside the root index.md. The page
# dots every occurrence of a term in its prose; hover shows the definition, and the
# glossary page lists each term with the claims that use it.
- term: trak # matched as a whole word, in any case
  aliases: [traks] # optional: the other ways the prose writes it; nothing looser matches
  definition: >- # a sentence or two, for a reader who knows the codebase but not this area
    One piece of work in orkestra, from the message that opened it to its last step.
- term: opening message
  definition: What the person wrote when they opened the trak, before any step ran.
```

## Fields

Every field, from the schema. A field marked *(optional)* may be left out.

### Record

A walkdown, as a folder: a record of one diff, `base..head`, or a snapshot of the code at one commit, `head` alone. Its `index.md` is the central claim, drawn as the top page, and the folder’s name is its id. Its header holds these fields, the record’s and the claim’s together. The top page opens on the slug, the title and line, then the header — a row of facts (diff or snapshot, the change’s kind, the commits, the pull requests), the motivation, and for a diff the change before and after in a sentence each — and the markdown under it is the top page’s body: the one figure that tells the change best.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `walkdown` | `1` | The format version. Always 1 for now. |
| `slug` | text | The page’s name: `publish` puts it at `<repository>/<slug>.html`, and the header strip draws it. Lowercase words joined by `-`. Keep it when the record is rewritten, so the page stays at the same address. |
| `base` | text *(optional)* | Where the change starts, as a full SHA: the record walks the diff from `base` to `head`, and every hunk id is numbered within it. For one commit it is that commit’s parent; for pull requests merged in a row, the commit before the first. Leave it out for a snapshot, which describes the code at `head` and has no diff. |
| `head` | text | The commit the record describes, as a full SHA: where the diff ends, or for a snapshot the code it walks, usually `HEAD` when the record is written. Source references are read here, and a published page opens with it. A record cannot name the commit that holds it, so one written before its pull request names the last commit before its own. |
| `prs` | list of text *(optional)* | Links to the pull requests the change went in by, in order, each drawn in the header as its number: `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/5043` reads `#5043`. A GitHub link also makes the commits links. Leave it out before there is one, or for a snapshot. |
| `change` | `fix`, `feature` or `refactor` *(optional)* | What kind of change this is, drawn in the header: `fix`, `feature` or `refactor`. Leave it out for a change that is none of them, and for a snapshot. |
| `motivation` | text | Why the change was made, in a sentence or two: the problem a reader would not know from the code. For a snapshot, why the record walks this code. Drawn first in the header, under the title, in a box of its own over `before` and `after`. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `before` | text *(optional)* | What was so before the change, in a sentence, drawn in the header in a box beside `after`, under the motivation. The top page's body carries the figure; this is the one-line version. A record with a `base` writes it; a snapshot does not. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `after` | text *(optional)* | What is so after the change, in a sentence. A record with a `base` writes it; a snapshot does not. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `questions` | list of text *(optional)* | The questions this record promises to answer, agreed with the person. The page never shows them; the crit reads them. |
| `context` | list of text *(optional)* | Where in the pipeline this claim’s code runs, as a breadcrumb of a few short parts from the outside in: `[nightly source sync, choosing which documents to re-read]`. Name the stage of the work, not the function that calls it. Drawn over the row’s address and over the page’s title, joined by `›` with the last part in ink. Give it wherever the area is not obvious to a reader who knows the codebase but not this part of it. |
| `title` | text | States the answer; the question is implied. “The step prompt opens on the instruction”, not “What changed in step.md”. An atlas entry is the exception: its title is its short name, `trak` or `plan`, because the atlas rail and the phone’s chips draw it and have room for no more, and its answer goes in its `line`. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `line` | text *(optional)* | One sentence under the title: a closed row shows its title and this line and nothing more. Leave it out only where the title says all there is, as for an item in a list of claims; a claim with a title alone, and no body, code or supporting claims, draws as its title on one row that opens nothing and keeps its kind. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `code` | list of text *(optional)* | The hunks this claim accounts for, folded by file at the foot of its page. `check` warns about hunks nothing names: not a claim’s `code`, a snippet or a flow step’s code. |
| `claims` | list of one of text, [Section](#section) | The supporting claims, by id, in the order they are drawn as rows, with an optional `- section: <heading>` item heading the rows after it. Each id names a `<id>.md` or a `<id>/` folder beside this `index.md`, and every claim file beside it is listed here. Only an `index.md` lists claims. |

### Claim

A statement with what supports it: its body, its code, and the claims under it. A claim with no supporting claims is one file, `<id>.md`. A claim with them is a folder, `<id>/`, holding its own `index.md` and a file or folder for each. The file or folder name is the claim’s id: unique across the whole record, and what flow steps name. Dots are fine: `step.lead.md`. The header between `---` lines holds these fields; the markdown under it is the body, and a fence opened with `yaml` and a figure type is a figure. A tradeoff, an open question, a risk, a breaking change or a measurement is a claim too, with a `kind`.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `tradeoff`, `open`, `risk`, `breaking` or `measured` *(optional)* | Leave it out for a plain claim. Give one when the claim is one of these, and its row is marked with the kind’s icon, word and tint. `tradeoff`: what was chosen, what was set aside, and what it costs. `open`: something left unfinished or unknown, and what would settle it. `risk`: where a bug would hide, what nothing tests or what is taken on trust, and how you would notice. `breaking`: behaviour that others relying on this will see change, and what they should do about it. `measured`: a check that was actually run — a timing, a sample of real records, a count — and what it found. Only `measured` says something was confirmed. |
| `context` | list of text *(optional)* | Where in the pipeline this claim’s code runs, as a breadcrumb of a few short parts from the outside in: `[nightly source sync, choosing which documents to re-read]`. Name the stage of the work, not the function that calls it. Drawn over the row’s address and over the page’s title, joined by `›` with the last part in ink. Give it wherever the area is not obvious to a reader who knows the codebase but not this part of it. |
| `title` | text | States the answer; the question is implied. “The step prompt opens on the instruction”, not “What changed in step.md”. An atlas entry is the exception: its title is its short name, `trak` or `plan`, because the atlas rail and the phone’s chips draw it and have room for no more, and its answer goes in its `line`. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `line` | text *(optional)* | One sentence under the title: a closed row shows its title and this line and nothing more. Leave it out only where the title says all there is, as for an item in a list of claims; a claim with a title alone, and no body, code or supporting claims, draws as its title on one row that opens nothing and keeps its kind. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `code` | list of text *(optional)* | The hunks this claim accounts for, folded by file at the foot of its page. `check` warns about hunks nothing names: not a claim’s `code`, a snippet or a flow step’s code. |
| `claims` | list of one of text, [Section](#section) *(optional)* | The supporting claims, by id, in the order they are drawn as rows, with an optional `- section: <heading>` item heading the rows after it. Each id names a `<id>.md` or a `<id>/` folder beside this `index.md`, and every claim file beside it is listed here. Only an `index.md` lists claims. |

### before-after

One text before and after the change, drawn whole and side by side (stacked on a phone), never as a diff, with nothing highlighted unless `whitespace` is `shown`; a `lang` colours both sides. The claim’s title and line say what to look at. For one text drawn as a diff with claims beside it, use an `excerpt` with a `before` and an `after`. To say in your own words what was so before and what is so after, use `shift`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml before-after ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `before` | [Side](#side) | The text before the change. |
| `after` | [Side](#side) | The same text after the change. |
| `lang` | text *(optional)* | The language the text is written in, as shiki names it: `sql`, `json`, `ruby`, `yaml`. `build` colours it as a code block is coloured. Leave it out for a text in no language, such as a prompt or a log line, which is drawn in ink. Both sides take it. |
| `how` | text *(optional)* | How the two texts were produced, drawn as a caption. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `whitespace` | `shown` *(optional)* | Write `shown` to draw invisible characters as glyphs — `·` a space, `→` a tab, `␍` a carriage return, `␊` a line feed, `⍽` a no-break space — and each text’s size in bytes. The characters one side has and the other does not are marked, from a character diff walkdown works out: use it when the change is in characters you cannot see, such as a line ending. Leave it out to draw both texts as written, with nothing marked. A claim file’s line endings are read as `\n`, so a `\r` reaches the text only as an escape in a double-quoted string: `text: "First\r\nSecond"`. |

### shift

A short summary of what this change moved: a Before panel and an After panel joined by an arrow, side by side (stacked on a phone). The labels are fixed, so write no bold Before. or After. lead-in. It means before and after this change and nothing else. To show one text as it was and as it is, verbatim, use `before-after`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml shift ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `before` | text | What was so before this change, in a sentence or two. Markdown. Write it as a `>-` block scalar, because in plain YAML ` #` starts a comment and a leading backtick is refused; a list needs `\|`, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `after` | text | What is so after this change, in a sentence or two. Markdown. Write it as a `>-` block scalar, because in plain YAML ` #` starts a comment and a leading backtick is refused; a list needs `\|`, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### excerpt

Source text with its provenance: where it lives and whether it was captured or derived. Given one `text` it is drawn as written; given a `before` and an `after`, as one diff. With `annotations` it is an annotated text, laid out as an annotated snippet is: the text on the left, and beside it a claim for each range of lines it explains, which lights that range as the reader points at it. Without them, the claim’s title and line say what matters in it.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml excerpt ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | text *(optional)* | The source text, verbatim: a log line, a prompt, a config file, a JSON object, a query plan. Write it, or a `before` and an `after`, never both. |
| `before` | text *(optional)* | The text as it was, verbatim, in place of `text`: with an `after`, the two are drawn as one diff, removed and added lines tinted and signed as a code block’s diff is, with one set of `annotations`. Lines match only when they are the same text, so a text whose every line changes, such as a query plan carrying timings, reads as the whole of it removed and then added. |
| `after` | text *(optional)* | The same text as it is, with `before`. |
| `src` | `captured` or `derived` | `captured` is text taken from a real run or file. `derived` was worked out by reading the code and is marked as such on the page. |
| `where` | text | Where this text lives or came from: the file, the log line, the store. |
| `lang` | text *(optional)* | The language the text is written in, as shiki names it: `sql`, `json`, `ruby`, `yaml`. `build` colours it as a code block is coloured. Leave it out for a text in no language, such as a prompt or a log line, which is drawn in ink. |
| `annotations` | list of [Text annotation](#text-annotation) *(optional)* | Supporting claims tied to ranges of the lines, drawn as their rows beside the text (under it on a phone), in the order of their lines, whatever order they are written in. Leave them out for a text that needs no pointing at. |
| `how` | text *(optional)* | How it was obtained or made, in one sentence, drawn as a caption. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `whitespace` | `shown` *(optional)* | Write `shown` to draw invisible characters as glyphs — `·` a space, `→` a tab, `␍` a carriage return, `␊` a line feed, `⍽` a no-break space — and each text’s size in bytes. Leave it out to draw the text as written. Only one `text`, with no `lang` and no `annotations`, shows its whitespace; for two texts, use `before-after`. A claim file’s line endings are read as `\n`, so a `\r` reaches the text only as an escape in a double-quoted string: `text: "First\r\nSecond"`. |

### cases

Named examples a reader picks between from a strip of buttons, as a flow’s lenses are picked, each one or more annotated texts stacked: a request over its response, for a cache hit and for a miss. No outcome is drawn: the case’s name and its annotations’ claims say how it came out. Use it where the reader learns how something behaves from seeing it go different ways. For one text, use `excerpt`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml cases ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `cases` | list of [Case](#case) | The examples, each a button above the figure, the first picked when the page opens. Pick ones that go different ways: a hit and a miss, a high score and a low one. |
| `how` | text *(optional)* | How the cases were captured or made, drawn as a caption. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### sketch

Pseudo-code for the whole change or snapshot, in the top page’s body only: drawn in a dashed box with no line numbers, so it cannot be read as real code, and its groups of lines annotated with claims that link to the real code each stands for. Use it where the code is spread over files and the reader needs the shape before the lines.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml sketch ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `outlines` | text | What it outlines, drawn in its head: `EvaluateWithJev, in outline`. |
| `text` | text | The pseudo-code, in the notation the `pseudo` skill sets out and coloured as a ```` ```pseudo ```` fence is: `x = value`, `each x in xs`, `if` / `else`, `while`, `return`; two-space indentation for blocks; a rules line such as `parallel, retries: 3` above the block it governs, and handlers such as `when: error` inside it; `{a hole}` for a step not worth spelling out; `#` for a comment. One statement to a line, and a call only for a name the code has. Keep it to a screen: it is an outline, not the code again. |
| `annotations` | list of [Text annotation](#text-annotation) | Supporting claims tied to ranges of the lines, drawn as their rows beside the text (under it on a phone), in the order of their lines, whatever order they are written in. Each claim is a group of lines: its title says what they do, and its `code` is the real code they stand for, drawn under its row as links to its page, so every claim here has `code`. |

### snippet

Code from the commit, drawn as it is after the change: removed lines left out, added lines on a green tint, the file’s line numbers beside them, and a `code | diff` switch in the head that shows the change. The text comes from git, never from the record. With `annotations` it is an annotated snippet: the code pinned on the left, and beside it a claim for each range it explains, which lights that range as the reader reaches it.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml snippet ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `code` | list of text | The code to show, each hunk id drawn as a block of its own. A slice cuts the hunk to the lines doing the work, and `⋯` stands for lines left out between its ranges. With `annotations`, name one. |
| `annotations` | list of [Annotation](#annotation) *(optional)* | Supporting claims tied to ranges of the lines, drawn as their rows beside the code (under it on a phone), in the order of their lines, whatever order they are written in. Leave them out for plain code between two paragraphs. |

### table

A table: a timeline, a list of surfaces, or anything with attributes to compare. Written out as `columns` and `rows`, or read from a CSV in the record folder as `data`, which may carry a bar or line chart. Use `data` for measurements and samples: the numbers are the evidence, and the table is where a reader checks them.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml table ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `columns` | list of text *(optional)* | Column headings. `Backtick` code draws as code. Leave every heading empty for a table with no heading row. Leave it out with `data`, whose first row is its headings. |
| `rows` | list of list of text *(optional)* | Rows; each has one cell per column. Leave it out with `data`. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `data` | text *(optional)* | A CSV file in the record folder, by path relative to the claim file the table is in, in place of `columns` and `rows`: its first row is the headings, and each cell is drawn as written, never as markdown. A column of numbers is set flush right in mono, its decimal points lined up. The file is the whole data or a sample of it, and it stays in the record folder, not the repository. `check` fails when it is missing or ragged, and `build` embeds it in the page. A long file scrolls in its own box. |
| `note` | text *(optional)* | With `data`, and only with it: one line saying what the file holds and, if it is a sample, how it was sampled: `sample: every 16th query by id, 240 of 3,912 rows`, or `full data: every query measured on this branch`. Drawn in the table’s head beside the file’s path. |
| `chart` | [Chart](#chart) *(optional)* | A bar or line chart drawn into the table from its data. Only a table with `data` has one. |
| `caption` | text *(optional)* | One line under the table. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### compare

Two or more options compared aspect by aspect: the aspect names in a grey column on the left, and the options facing each other across one line down the middle, each answer a short verdict in mono with a mark and the whole answer under it. Peers are compared with no winner; mark one option `chosen` and it is a decision, its options set aside each facing it in turn, the aspect each was set aside on tinted red. Use it in place of a `table` whose columns are the options and whose rows are what tells them apart.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml compare ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `heading` | text *(optional)* | What is compared, a few words drawn in the figure’s bar after `COMPARE`: `where each part of the feature lives`. |
| `options` | list of [Compare option](#compare-option) | The options, in order. With more than two, a strip of lenses in the figure’s bar picks what faces the left one: all of them at once, the first open, or one at a time. |
| `aspects` | list of [Aspect](#aspect) | The aspects the options differ on, each a row, in the order written: the one that decides it first. |
| `shared` | list of [Shared aspect](#shared-aspect) *(optional)* | What the options have in common, so the reader sees what does not differ too. Leave it out when nothing does. |
| `cost` | text *(optional)* | In a decision: what the chosen option costs, in a sentence, drawn under the figure as `COST`. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### atlas

Some of this claim’s supporting claims laid out as entries a reader browses: a rail of their names, under group headings, beside one full card for the entry picked, in one frame. The card holds the tallest entry’s height, so picking another swaps only its content; its header names the entry’s group and steps through the entries, `‹ 2 / 8 ›`. A card draws the entry’s name, line and evidence, its value for each attribute, the first paragraph of its body, its files, an excerpt of its code and a link to its page. On a phone the rail is a row of chips over the same card. Use it where a claim’s parts are peers a reader explores one at a time, such as the components of a system, rather than steps in an order, which is a `flow`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml atlas ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `heading` | text *(optional)* | What the entries are, a few words drawn in the figure’s bar after `ATLAS` and the count: `Orkestra’s key components`. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `attributes` | list of text *(optional)* | The names of what every entry is described by, in the order the card draws them, each a mono label beside its value: `[Declared in, Runs, Ends or fails]`. No two the same. Leave them out and the card draws none. |
| `entries` | list of [Atlas entry](#atlas-entry) | The entries, in the order the rail lists them and the reader steps through them. The first is picked when the page opens. |

### image

A drawing no other figure can express: a screenshot, or an SVG you drew. Embedded HTML is not a figure. For several screenshots of one change, use `gallery`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml image ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `src` | text | A PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG file, by path relative to the claim file the figure is in. `check` fails when it is missing, and `build` embeds it in the page. |
| `alt` | text | The sentence you would have written without the picture. |
| `caption` | text *(optional)* | One line under the image. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### gallery

A set of screenshots of one change, in named groups: widths, states, before and after. A click on a shot opens it full screen, where the arrow keys step through every shot of the gallery in the order written and the picture can be seen at one file pixel per screen pixel. For one picture, use `image`.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml gallery ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `groups` | list of [Shot group](#shot-group) | The groups, in order, each under its own heading. Group by what the shots show together — a state, a width — so the heading says it once. A single group is fine. |

### flow

A value followed through some of this claim’s supporting claims, its steps, with hops between them. A flow with no fork, join or loop is drawn as a numbered rail. A flow whose first step has a hop to every other step, with no hop anywhere else and no hop labelled, is drawn as a fan: one value and everything that reads it, the start pinned beside its readers, which are unnumbered and in the order written; a `breaking` reader is one the value damages. Anything else, and a fan with `spans`, is drawn as a map beside the steps. A claim has at most one flow or walkthrough.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml flow ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `steps` | list of one of text, [Label step](#label-step) | The steps, in order: each the id of one of this claim’s own supporting claims, once, or a label step. The first is the start. Supporting claims left out are drawn after the body, under “Not in the flow”. |
| `hops` | list of [Hop](#hop) *(optional)* | The arrows between steps. Leave them out and the steps are joined in the order listed. Every step has to be reachable from the start; no hop joins a step to itself, and none is written twice. |
| `spans` | list of [Span](#span) *(optional)* | Scopes over runs of steps, each drawn as a box around the steps it holds: a transaction, a lock, a request. A span that holds another is drawn around it; of two that hold the same steps, the one written first is drawn outside. A flow shaped as a fan that has spans is drawn as a map. |
| `lenses` | list of [Lens](#lens) *(optional)* | Named subsets of the flow a reader can pick, each drawn as a button above it; the first is picked when the page opens. Use them in place of a table that traces inputs through the flow. A flow with a fork has them, one way through to a lens; a fan need not. Leave them out of a flow with no fork and the whole flow is its one lens, with no buttons. |
| `payload` | text *(optional)* | The data the whole flow carries, when it has no `lenses`: with lenses, each lens names its own. A payload file, by path relative to the claim file the flow is in: `payloads/crlf-edit.yaml`. Its fields are under [Payload file](#payload-file). `check` fails when it is missing and reads it with the record. |
| `code` | map of text to [Step code](#step-code) *(optional)* | The code each step runs, by the step’s name as a hop names it: `guard.size: { lines: [app/x.rb#2:30-33], key: [app/x.rb#2:33] }`. A step left out draws no code. A flow carries code or payloads, never both: with code, neither the flow nor any lens names a `payload`. |

### walkthrough

A decision, walked one question at a time: the reader reads a step, picks one of its options, and goes on to the step it leads to, until an outcome. A trail over the step goes back to any step already passed, and a line over the step names the last pick and changes it. Beside the step, its table: every cell its type or range until a pick pins it, with what the step reads and writes tinted; each outcome shows its example. Use it where the reader’s question is which way something goes and why, and a flow where it is what happens to a thing, in what order. A claim has at most one flow or walkthrough.

Written as a fence: ```` ```yaml walkthrough ````.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `steps` | list of one of text, [Label step](#label-step) | The steps, as a flow’s are: each the id of one of this claim’s own supporting claims, once, or a label step. The first is where the walk starts; a step with no option out is an outcome. A claim step draws its claim’s title, line and markdown body, so write that body as a short list of how the step works. |
| `hops` | list of [Option](#option) | The options out of each step, in the order their cards are drawn. Every step has to be reachable from the start, and no option leads back. A step has three options at most. |
| `code` | map of text to [Key lines](#key-lines) *(optional)* | The key lines each step runs, by the step’s name as an option names it: `score: { key: [app/jev.rb#3:12] }`. A step left out draws no code. |
| `table` | text *(optional)* | The table the decision reads and writes. A table file, by path relative to the claim file the walkthrough is in: `tables/route.yaml`. Its fields are under [Walkthrough table](#walkthrough-table). `check` fails when it is missing and reads it with the record. |

### Payload file

Example data followed through a flow: what goes in, the payload after each step, and what comes out. A YAML file of its own, not a claim file, beside the claim whose flow names it; a folder holding only payload files is not a claim. The page reads it in the lens’s column: the input under `START`, each stage under its step’s row and before its code, with only what changed drawn and the rest folded, and the outcome after `END`. Round a loop, the column reads on: a step the payload reaches again is a back-line with its stage, and one it first reaches on a later run is drawn in full.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `input` | [Payload input](#payload-input) *(optional)* | What goes in. |
| `stages` | list of [Payload stage](#payload-stage) | The payload after each step it passes, in the order it passes them. It is diffed against the stage whose step hands it on: on a chain the stage before, on a fan the input. |
| `outcome` | text *(optional)* | What came of it, drawn as `OUT` after the last stage. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Walkthrough table

The data a walkthrough decides on, as a table of rows and typed columns with fields over and under it, what each step reads and writes, and one real example per outcome. A YAML file of its own beside the claim whose walkthrough names it; a folder holding only table files is not a claim. The page pins it beside the step: each cell shows its range or type until a pick narrows it.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `input` | list of [Table field](#table-field) *(optional)* | What the decision is given, each on a line over the table: `query`. |
| `heading` | text *(optional)* | The heading over the rows’ names, `candidate`. Leave it out for none. |
| `columns` | list of [Table column](#table-column) | The columns, in order. |
| `rows` | list of [Table row](#table-row) | The rows, in order. |
| `fields` | list of [Table field](#table-field) *(optional)* | Values the decision works out, each on a line under the table: `route`. |
| `steps` | map of text to [Step marks](#step-marks) *(optional)* | What each step reads and writes, by the step’s name as an option names it. Table addresses are as `narrows` writes them. |
| `examples` | map of text to [Example](#example) *(optional)* | One real case for each outcome, by the outcome’s name as an option names it: drawn under the outcome when the walk reaches it. An outcome reached by more than one option can have one for each, keyed by the option as `from → to`: `any evidence kept? → no_match`. The walk shows the one for the option it took, or else the outcome’s own. |

### Glossary term

One word the record defines. `glossary.yaml`, beside the root `index.md`, is a YAML list of these; leave the file out for a record with no terms. The page marks every occurrence of a term or an alias in its prose with a dotted underline: titles, lines, context, bodies, captions, `how`, table cells, the header and a payload’s `does`, and an inline code span whose whole text is a term. Code, map stations and hop labels are never marked. Hover shows the definition, a tap does on a phone, and the glossary page lists every term with the claims that use it. `check` refuses a word two entries claim and warns about a term the record never uses.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `term` | text | The word or phrase, as the record writes it: `manual_edit`, `source sync`. It is matched wherever the page draws prose, as a whole word and in any case. Code-styled on the glossary page when it looks like an identifier. |
| `aliases` | list of text *(optional)* | Other ways the record writes the same thing, each matched as the term is: `[manually edited, manual edit]`. Only these are matched, never a looser form, so list each inflection the prose uses. A word may belong to one entry only. |
| `definition` | text | What the term means here, in a sentence or two, for a reader who knows the codebase but not this area. Shown in the card over a marked word and on the glossary page. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Section

A heading over the rows listed after it, up to the next section: written `- section: What breaks` among the ids. It heads rows only, never the body or a flow’s steps, so `check` refuses one with no row under it. Rows listed before the first section have no heading.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `section` | text | The heading, a few words. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |

### Side

The text before the change.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | text | The whole text on this side, verbatim. Elide with a `[…]` line. |
| `where` | text | Where this side’s text came from: the file and commit, the log line, the store. Drawn under the side’s label. |

### Text annotation

A supporting claim tied to a range of a text’s lines: an excerpt’s, a case block’s or a sketch’s.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `lines` | one of number, text | The lines it is about, counted from 1 down the text as it is drawn: `3-5`, or one line, `3`. For a `before` and an `after`, count the diff’s lines, removed and added alike, as `walkdown read` numbers them. |
| `claim` | text | One of this claim’s supporting claims, drawn as its row beside the text, level with these lines, which light while the row is pointed at, as an annotated snippet’s rows do: it is not drawn again under the rows, and it may not also be a flow step or another annotation’s claim. |

### Case

One real example the figure shows: a different input, not the same input drawn another way.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What tells this case from the others, in a few words: `cache hit`, `miss: a different date`. Drawn on its button. No other case of the figure may use it. |
| `blocks` | list of [Case block](#case-block) | Its texts, stacked in the order written: a request over its response. |

### Annotation

A supporting claim tied to a range of a snippet’s lines.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `lines` | one of number, text | The lines it is about, as `walkdown hunks` numbers the hunk’s printed lines: `30-31`, or one line, `30`. They are inside the snippet’s slice. The page tags the row with the file’s own line numbers, `L91–92`, and lights these lines when the row is pointed at. |
| `claim` | text | One of this claim’s supporting claims, drawn as its row beside the code, which stays pinned as the rows scroll past and lights these lines while the row is read, as a flow’s map follows its steps: it is not drawn again under the rows, and it may not also be a flow step or another annotation’s claim. |

### Chart

A chart drawn into a data table from its own columns. It holds no data, so `walkdown read` prints the table it is drawn from.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `bar` or `line` | `bar` draws a bar under each number of the `series` columns, all on one scale, so the numbers compare across the row and down the column. `line` draws a row under the table with a line for each series down the rows, in the order written, each scaled to its own largest value and labelled with it: for counts over time. |
| `series` | list of text | The columns drawn, by heading: one or two of the data’s numeric columns. The first is drawn blue, the second amber. |
| `scale` | `linear` or `log` *(optional)* | How a bar’s length follows its number: `log` where the numbers span orders of magnitude, so a small one still shows, and the head says so. Linear when left out. A line is always linear. |

### Compare option

One of the things compared: a peer, or in a decision the chosen option or one set aside.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | The option, in a few words: `Global rule`, `All in SourceTransforms`. Drawn over its column, and on its lens button. No other option of the figure may use it. |
| `chosen` | `true` *(optional)* | Write `true` on the option that was picked, and the figure is a decision: the chosen option stands on the left and each option set aside faces it on the right. One option at most. Leave it out of every option to compare peers, the first written on the left. |
| `fails` | text *(optional)* | On an option set aside, in a decision: the aspect it was set aside on, by its `name`. Its cell there is tinted red. |
| `because` | text *(optional)* | On an option set aside, in a decision: why, in a sentence, drawn under the figure as `SET ASIDE BECAUSE` while this option faces the chosen one. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Aspect

One row of a comparison: an aspect the options differ on.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What is compared, in a few words: `Runs`, `Managed from`, `Covers a new podcast source`. Drawn in the grey column on the left. No other aspect of the figure, shared or not, may use it. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `cells` | list of [Compare cell](#compare-cell) | One answer per option, in the order the options are written. |

### Shared aspect

An aspect every option has in common, drawn as a row across the options after the rows that differ.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What is the same, in a few words: `Claims`, `Display URL`. Drawn as an aspect is. |
| `explanation` | text | How it works for every option, in a line, drawn across them. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Atlas entry

One entry of an atlas: a supporting claim, the group it is listed under, its value for each attribute, and the lines of code that show it.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `claim` | text | One of this claim’s own supporting claims, drawn as this entry: its title is the entry’s name in the rail and on the card, its line is drawn under the name, then its kind, address and evidence, the first paragraph of its body, the files its `code` names, and a link that opens its page. It is not drawn again under the rows, and it may not also be a flow step, an annotation’s claim or another entry. |
| `group` | text *(optional)* | The group it is listed under: a heading over its run of names in the rail, and the card’s header while it is picked. Either every entry of the atlas names a group or none does, and a group’s entries are written one after another. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `values` | map of text to text *(optional)* | Its value for each of the atlas’s `attributes`, by the attribute’s name: `Runs: One session per step`. An attribute left out is drawn as `—`. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in a value. |
| `excerpt` | text *(optional)* | A few lines of its code that show what it is, as a hunk id or a source reference, drawn on the card as a code block under its files. Slice it to the lines that show it: a type’s fields, a config’s keys. Leave it out where no few lines do. |

### Shot group

A named set of shots in a gallery.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What the group’s shots have in common, in a few words: `Scrolling`, `At 390px`. Drawn as the group’s heading in mono capitals, with its count of shots. |
| `caption` | text *(optional)* | One line under the group’s heading. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `shots` | list of [Shot](#shot) | The group’s shots in order: three across on a wide page, one across on a phone. |

### Label step

A flow step that is words rather than a claim: the value a fan starts from, or a point the flow passes. It has no number, no address and no evidence, and opens nothing unless it names a `claim`. In a rail it is an unnumbered row; on a map, a station with no address.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | text | The words on the step, drawn in mono: a value such as `manual_edit = true`, or a point the flow passes that no claim is about. Hops name the step by these words, so no other step of the flow may use them. |
| `where` | text *(optional)* | Where the value lives or comes from, drawn under the label: `app/models/document.rb:88`. |
| `claim` | text *(optional)* | One of this claim’s supporting claims, whose page a click on the label opens. It may not also be a step, and it may not be a leaf, which has no page to open. It counts as in the flow, so it is not drawn under “Not in the flow”. Leave it out and the label opens nothing. |

### Hop

An arrow from one step of a flow to another.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `from` | text | The step the hop leaves: one of this flow’s `steps`, by its claim id or a label step’s `label`. |
| `to` | text | The step the hop reaches, named as `from` names one. A hop back to a step on the way to `from` is a loop, drawn dashed. |
| `label` | text *(optional)* | A word or two for the branch: `artifact`, `send back`. Written on the arrow on the map; the steps say nothing of it, so a step whose claim is about the choice explains it in its own words. |

### Span

A scope some steps of a flow run inside, such as a database transaction: drawn as a box around them, named on a tab. A span may sit inside another, and the two may share a first or last step; spans that only partly overlap are refused.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What the scope is, a word or two: `transaction`, `Document#save`. Drawn in mono on a tab in the box’s top edge. No other span of the flow may use it. |
| `line` | text *(optional)* | A short line after the name on the tab: `logidze.meta set`. The map’s tab drops it, and a long one is cut short with an ellipsis. |
| `steps` | list of text | The steps it holds, each named as a hop names one: a run of steps next to each other in reading order, with nothing between them left out. On a map it holds whole ranks, so a step drawn beside one it holds is held too: a span cannot hold one side of a fork and not the other. |

### Lens

A named subset of a flow that a reader picks from the buttons above it: its steps and hops stay lit on the map and the rest fade, and the column draws only its steps. It takes one side of each fork it passes, on each run: a second run round a loop may take another. `START` marks its first step in reading order and `END` each lit step with no lit hop out; a fan has no `START`. It may carry one payload.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | What the lens picks out, a few words: `CRLF edit`, `what broke`. Drawn on its button above the flow. No other lens of the flow may use it. |
| `steps` | list of text | The steps it lights, each named as a hop names one. They need not be a connected route: on a fan they are readers, and the start is always lit. |
| `hops` | list of [Lens hop](#lens-hop) *(optional)* | The hops it lights, each one of the flow’s hops between two of its steps. Leave them out and it lights the hops its payload’s stages take, or with no payload every hop whose two ends it lights. Write them when a fork rejoins and the case took one side: lighting both ends would light the other side too. |
| `payload` | text *(optional)* | The data this lens carries. A payload file, by path relative to the claim file the flow is in: `payloads/crlf-edit.yaml`. Its fields are under [Payload file](#payload-file). `check` fails when it is missing and reads it with the record. |
| `again` | map of text to text *(optional)* | What a step does differently when the lens's payload comes round a loop to it again, by the step's name as a hop names it: `route.turn: Resumes the session instead of starting one.` Each one a step the payload reaches again on a later run. Drawn under that step's back-line. Leave a step out and its back-line stands alone. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Step code

The code a flow step runs: all of it, and the key lines a map shows, or the key lines alone. It names `lines`, `key` or both.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `lines` | list of text *(optional)* | The step’s code: hunk ids, sliced to what the step does. Drawn in full under the step’s row in a rail, a map’s reading column and a fan. Leave it out to draw only the `key` lines, in all three places and on the station: a line or two is what the reader takes in beside a flow. |
| `key` | list of text *(optional)* | One to three of those lines that do the work, as hunk ids again: each one a hunk `lines` names, and inside its slice. A map’s station draws them under its title, and grows to hold them; on a phone they sit in a box under the stop bar. Written without `lines`, they are the step’s whole code, drawn wherever `lines` would be. Leave it out and the station stays a compact box with no code. |

### Option

One way out of a walkthrough step, drawn as a card the reader picks: its label, its rule, what it means, and where it leads.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `from` | text | The step the option leaves: one of this walkthrough’s `steps`, by its claim id or a label step’s `label`. |
| `to` | text | The step taking it leads to, named as `from` names one. A walkthrough never goes back: no option reaches a step on the way to `from`. |
| `label` | text *(optional)* | A word or two naming the option, `applies`, `none kept`: drawn large on its card, and on the line over the next step as the pick. Every option out of a step with two or more has one; a step with one option draws it as `continue`. |
| `rule` | text *(optional)* | The test that sends the walk this way, as the code states it: `applicability ≥ 0.45 and mismatch < 0.50`. Drawn in mono on the card, and after the pick on the line over the next step. |
| `means` | text *(optional)* | What taking this option means, in a sentence on its card. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `narrows` | map of text to text *(optional)* | What taking it pins down in the table, by table address: `answer 1.applicability: "≥ 0.45"`, `relevance: "< 0.50"`, `answer 1.verdict: applies`. A table address is a row and a column joined by `.`, a whole column, a whole row, or a field. The pinned text replaces the cell’s placeholder from the next step on; a later pick pinning the same cell wins. Write it yourself: the page never works it out from `rule`, since only you know which row fails which way. |

### Key lines

The code a walkthrough step runs, as its key lines only.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | list of text | One to three lines that do the step’s work, as hunk ids sliced to them. Drawn under the step’s text, as a map’s station draws its key lines. |

### Payload input

What enters the flow, drawn as `IN` beside `START`.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | text *(optional)* | The value going in, as one short line of mono: `` `raw: "First\r\nThird"` ``. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `data` | any JSON value *(optional)* | The payload going in: any JSON value, written as YAML. Drawn pretty-printed. |

### Payload stage

The payload after one step. Stages are in the order the payload travels, and a stage’s place in that order is what the page goes by.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `step` | text | The step this stage is the payload after, named as a hop names one. It is in the lens, and a hop from an earlier stage’s step reaches it. A step taken twice, round a loop, is two stages: each pass is its own. Keep a stage at every lit step the payload passes, including a second pass that repeats the first. |
| `does` | text *(optional)* | What the step does to the payload, or decides about it, in a sentence under the value. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |
| `value` | text *(optional)* | The value as it leaves the step, as one short line of mono. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `data` | any JSON value *(optional)* | The whole payload as it leaves the step: any JSON value, written as YAML. It is drawn diffed against the payload the step received. Leave it out when the step changes nothing. |
| `table` | [Stage table](#stage-table) *(optional)* | The payload as it leaves the step, as a table in place of `data`: a stage has one or the other. Leave it out when the step changes nothing. |

### Table field

One value drawn on a line of its own.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | The field’s name, as table addresses name it: `answerable`. |
| `holds` | text | What it holds, `string`, drawn in italics as its placeholder. |
| `range` | text *(optional)* | The range it can take, `0 – 1`, drawn as the placeholder in place of what it holds. |

### Table column

A column of a walkthrough’s table.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | The column’s name, as table addresses name it: `applicability`. No `.` in it, since a table address joins a row and a column with one. |
| `head` | text *(optional)* | A shorter heading to draw, `applic.`. Leave it out to draw the name. |
| `holds` | text | What the cells hold, `probability`, drawn in italics as a cell’s placeholder. |
| `range` | text *(optional)* | The range the cells can take, `0 – 1`, drawn as the placeholder in place of what it holds. |

### Table row

A row of a walkthrough’s table.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | text | The row’s name, drawn first: `answer 1`, `chunk 2`. |
| `cells` | list of text *(optional)* | The columns this row has, by name; the rest are drawn `—`. Leave it out for every column. |

### Step marks

What one step of a walkthrough reads and writes, as table addresses.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `reads` | list of text *(optional)* | The table addresses the step reads, tinted coral while it is the step on screen. |
| `writes` | list of text *(optional)* | The table addresses the step writes, tinted green while it is the step on screen. |

### Example

One real case that reaches an outcome.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `input` | text | A real input that goes this way, drawn quoted: `When does the pool close?`. |
| `values` | text *(optional)* | The values that sent it here, in one line of mono: `A301: applicability 0.88, mismatch 0.10`. |
| `outcome` | text *(optional)* | What came of it, in a sentence. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Case block

One text of a case, drawn as an excerpt is: a request, or the response under it.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | text | The text, verbatim: a request, a response, a row, a log line. |
| `src` | `captured` or `derived` | `captured` is text taken from a real run or file. `derived` was worked out by reading the code and is marked as such on the page. |
| `where` | text | Where this text came from, drawn in its head: `Jev::Request · turn t_91c4`. |
| `lang` | text *(optional)* | The language the text is written in, as shiki names it: `sql`, `json`, `ruby`, `yaml`. `build` colours it as a code block is coloured. Leave it out for a text in no language, such as a prompt or a log line, which is drawn in ink. |
| `annotations` | list of [Text annotation](#text-annotation) *(optional)* | Supporting claims tied to ranges of the lines, drawn as their rows beside the text (under it on a phone), in the order of their lines, whatever order they are written in. |

### Compare cell

One option’s answer on one aspect: its verdict, a mark, and the whole of it.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `verdict` | text | The answer, in a few words: `yes`, `MCP only`, `before every source rule`. Drawn in mono, so a reader takes in the row from its verdicts. Backtick code is the only markdown drawn in it. |
| `mark` | `yes`, `no` or `mixed` *(optional)* | A mark beside the verdict, on a small square of its tint: `yes` a green ✓, `no` a red ✕, `mixed` a ◐. A mark judges the option, and a ✕ reads as a failing, so give one only where an option can pass or fail the aspect; leave it out for a plain fact, such as which of two peers runs first. |
| `explanation` | text *(optional)* | The whole answer, drawn under the verdict in small muted type. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Shot

One screenshot in a gallery group: its label, its file and its alt.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | text | What tells this shot from the others in its group, in a few words: `businesses · 1440`, `empty`. Drawn over the picture in mono capitals. |
| `src` | text | A PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG file, by path relative to the claim file the figure is in. `check` fails when it is missing, and `build` embeds it in the page. |
| `alt` | text | The sentence you would have written without the picture. |
| `caption` | text *(optional)* | What to look at in this shot, drawn under it when it is opened full screen; the gallery itself shows no per-shot caption. Markdown, lists included. A list needs a `\|` block scalar, because `>-` folds line breaks into spaces. A link to `#` and a claim’s id is a reference, `[the size guard](#guard.size)`: it may name any claim in the record, and a click opens that claim. |

### Lens hop

One of the flow’s hops, lit under the lens: its `from` and `to`, without its label.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `from` | text | The step the hop leaves, named as a hop of the flow names it. |
| `to` | text | The step the hop reaches. |

### Stage table

A payload stage drawn as a table: a row per candidate and a column per score, for a step that scores several things at once, where the same data as JSON runs a screen tall. A cell that differs from the same row and column in the table the step received is tinted as added.

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `columns` | list of text | Column headings, the first over the rows’ names: `[candidate, applicability, mismatch, kept]`. No two the same. |
| `rows` | list of list of one of text, number, `true` or `false` | One row per candidate, each one cell per column, its name first: `[answer 1, 0.88, 0.10, kept]`. No two rows share a name. A cell is drawn as written, in mono; a column of numbers is set flush right. |
